notes: Source atlases store bands; runtime joins twelve whole depictions into one linear cloth. Opening uses only corrected band 1. Original early atlas supplies unchanged bands 2–4; lower bands in the opening edit are unused.

early.prompt:
Use case: historical-scene.
Asset type: production source atlas for ONE continuous linear Bayeux tapestry in Paper Trails, a scientific-history timeline. The supplied image is the mandatory STYLE reference, not subjects to copy indiscriminately.
Create a wide landscape image with EXACTLY FOUR long horizontal embroidered bands stacked top to bottom as a source atlas, overall image 3:1 aspect. Each band is ONE single connected left-to-right scene, about twelve times as wide as high, between narrow continuous animal and bird borders. These four storage bands will be joined end to end in the application into ONE LINEAR STRIP, never displayed as a multirow collage. No separate vignette boxes, no floating motifs, no scenic thumbnails. Adjacent band endings and beginnings must join on bare linen and a single thin stitched ground at the same vertical position. Continuous warm pale linen, uniform figure scale and thread palette in every band.
Match the reference VERY CLOSELY: exposed flax linen, vivid madder red / ochre / indigo / sage wool stem-stitch contours, flat laid-and-couched thread fills, unfilled profile faces, angular expressive limbs/hands, sparse symbolic architecture. This is embroidery, not painting: no photographic detail, tonal gradients, volumetric shading, filled skies, black ink or sepia wash. Figures large relative to band height. Upper and lower border alternating embroidered birds, deer, dogs and leaf sprigs. Keep all figures within borders.
Four chronological bands, top to bottom:
1. 1380–1500: late medieval scholarship and Renaissance awakening as one scene: a manor rent exchange at left, scholars sharing manuscripts with a painter and geometric drawing in the central group, then a printer turning a press with apprentices carrying books at right. Mostly open linen, one baseline, restrained symbolic arcaded building, period clothing.
2. 1500–1600: Reformation pamphlets and religious debate, Renaissance study and Atlantic coercion overlap in one depiction: scholars and printers at left; a reformer holding a book with disputing townspeople in centre; African coastal community, a guarded forced embarkation and a sailing vessel at right. Convey agency, distress and dignity without gore. No modern flags or weapons. Interweave figures and shared objects, don't divide scenes into panels.
3. 1600–1650: Little Ice Age snow, Thirty Years' War and English Civil War IN THE SAME DRAWN SCENE: a snow-covered bare tree and family carrying firewood, pikemen crossing the same snowy ground behind a cart, a cannon and roundhead/cavalier figures interacting by a symbolic fortified gate, sparse chilly weather stitches above. Snow threads run under every subject, winter is part of the setting, not a separate winter vignette. Period muskets and clothing.
4. 1650–1700: continuing cold period, famine and Atlantic plantation labour/resistance as one continuous scene: a cold village household sharing a small loaf and hauling fuel at left, hungry people near poor grain at centre, an Atlantic ship connects toward Black families/community and plantation workers who also organise mutual aid at right. Geographic transition symbolic, no causal claim that climate caused enslavement; dignity, no gore. Shared baseline and connected threads. End with a bare vine/tree on exposed linen.
No words, letters, numerals, dates, captions or watermark anywhere. No repeated people or cloned panels. No layout UI. Every band must be a coherent single depiction with its contemporaneous subjects drawn together, not separate cutouts. Keep first main identifying action group close enough to the left to remain visible when later detail is pleated behind it.

opening.prompt: Edit this production atlas. Keep bands 2, 3 and 4, their borders, linen, figures, exact positions and style unchanged. Change ONLY the artwork of band 1 to cover the missing important subjects in the historical sequence. It must remain ONE connected Bayeux embroidered narrative on a single ground, with the same continuous bird/animal borders and scale. Left-to-right band 1: Renaissance manuscript scholarship and a painter with a geometric drawing in the first quarter; the 1453 fall of Constantinople represented by a sparse symbolic Byzantine city gateway, an Ottoman officer in fifteenth-century dress and a cannon in the middle; then an early Atlantic sailing ship, maize and plants carried by people with Indigenous American people shown with dignity at the right, representing the early Columbian Exchange after 1492. Retain mostly exposed linen and flat coloured wool thread grammar, profile faces, expressive hands and restrained architecture. No realistic filled background. Do not imply that Constantinople's fall caused the Atlantic exchange: these successive subjects share a narrative ground, not an explanatory arrow. No text, numerals, labels or watermarks. Preserve all three lower bands exactly.

middle.prompt: Use case: precise-object-edit. Edit target is the FIRST supplied image, the entire 2172 by 724 pixel four-band embroidered production atlas. The SECOND image is a close-up identifying the anatomical mistake, not a replacement image. Make exactly one small correction: in the fourth/bottom narrative band, near 40 percent of the atlas width, the startled male telegraph operator in a dark blue Victorian coat beneath the sparking telegraph wires has THREE arms. Remove the extra raised hand and its extra forearm immediately in front of/above his face, restoring pale linen and the existing background thread lines behind it. He must have exactly TWO arms: keep the existing leftmost arm bent forward with an open hand toward the spark, and keep the existing arm extending down and behind his right hip with its hand. Preserve his head, face, coat, stance and these two retained arms. Make the tiny repaired area match the flat Bayeux wool-thread contours and exposed linen texture seamlessly. Keep the rest of the entire atlas absolutely unchanged: all four bands, every other person/object, figures' positions, telegraph network and aurora, Napoleon, engine, animal borders, exact crop boundaries and 2172x724 dimensions. No redesign, new letters, captions, dates, new limbs or new subjects. Return the full atlas, not the close-up.
middle.correction: Remove the telegraph operator's extra arm; retain exactly two arms and the shared scene.

supportingReference.role: user close-up identifying the unwanted third arm

previousGeneration.prompt:
Use case: historical-scene. Production source atlas for Paper Trails' continuous folded Bayeux narrative. Match the supplied STYLE reference VERY CLOSELY: pale exposed woven flax linen, vivid madder/ochre/indigo/sage coloured wool stem-stitch contours, flat laid-and-couched wool fills, unfilled profile faces, angular expressive limbs and hands. Sparse symbolic architecture, one thin embroidered ground baseline. No tonal shading, photographic detail, painterly washes, perspective depth or filled skies. Figures and objects large relative to band height. EXACTLY FOUR connected very long horizontal bands stacked TOP TO BOTTOM, overall wide landscape 3:1 aspect; each band about twelve times as wide as high with narrow continuous animal/bird/plant borders at top and bottom. These four bands are STORAGE ONLY; they will join END TO END into ONE single linear cloth, never be displayed as a row collage. Each band is one drawn scene, with concurrent events inhabiting the SAME PICTURE: no independent vignettes, montage boxes, floating objects, separate vertical lanes or large empty holes. Keep scale, ground and border heights identical, begin/end each band on plain linen with sparse leaf sprigs for coherent end-to-end joins. No letters, numerals, labels, dates, watermark or gore. No cloned people/panels. Do not copy the reference's industrial subjects into unrelated epochs.
FOUR BANDS IN THIS ORDER:
1. 1700–1740: snowy winter setting ties the War of Spanish Succession and Great Frost together in one depiction: early eighteenth-century officers and musketeers, a cannon being drawn by a horse, a courier, cold village families chopping fuel, an icebound canal boat, frosted trees. Officer/cannon cluster toward the LEFT, then frozen village woven into the SAME ground, and continuing cold winter travel toward right. No medieval dress.
2. 1740–1789: snowy countryside softens into the Seven Years' War and industrialising workshops, then the American Revolution and Constitution. A large eighteenth-century cannon and soldiers at left; a water wheel, textile worker and recognisable beam steam engine occupy the same connected setting in centre; American militia and revolutionary delegates with an unsigned parchment at right. Snow and factories interweave rather than independent boxes. Colonial/revolutionary dress, no modern flags.
3. 1789–1830: revolutionary France, Haiti, Napoleon and steam power composed into one long drawing: a French crowd and tricolour with revolutionary figures at left; dignified Black Haitian organisers and revolutionary figures in period dress connected by an Atlantic sailing ship; a strongly recognisable Napoleon with bicorne and hand-in-coat STANDING NEXT TO a large beam steam engine and its worker in centre; a snow-dusted road carries artillery and an early locomotive toward right. Napoleon and steam machinery must read together immediately. Concurrent context woven in same picture, transitions express succession along the shared baseline, not causal connections between all subjects. No modern buildings, no medieval peasants.
4. 1830–1870: ONE continuous telegraph network stretches across the scene: large poles and copper wires connect a Victorian key operator, batteries, spark at a disconnected battery and restrained aurora thread loops OVER THE SAME WIRES. Make Carrington and the telegraph disruption one compelling central action group, never separate aurora thumbnail. At left a receding cold bare tree and Victorian village, not ongoing snow on the later right. At right a cable-laying shore station joins an American Civil War artillery/team and abolition campaigners in historically appropriate 1860s dress. Wired communication literally threads these connected objects together. No false date labels. Operator and wire sparks near LEFT-CENTRE so it stays identifiable folded.

The rocket should be large and obvious. Machinery is coloured wool with visible stitching, never black painted realism.

Keep modern subject depiction consistent with the original Bayeux style: angular profile humans, flat stitched machines, very little background, abundant exposed linen, continuous animals above/below.
